title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Ops Playbook (Consolidated)
author: Alex Kim
body:
Summary:
This consolidated guide documents Redwood Inference's serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling design, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, release-note conventions, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended as the canonical reference for engineers troubleshooting performance, planning kernel/scheduler changes, or preparing releases.

Audience:
- Serving runtime engineers
- SREs oncall for inference clusters
- Model onboarding and performance engineering teams
- Release managers for runtime and platform updates

Goals:
- Provide a single, searchable source of truth for runtime architecture and scheduler behaviour.
- Standardize profiling and benchmarking procedures so results are comparable across releases.
- Give operational runbooks for common incidents and escalation paths.

1) Runtime architecture (high level)
Intro:
The serving runtime is a modular, GPU-optimized inference engine designed for low-latency, high-throughput LLM serving. Core components are: request router, request transformer, batching manager, kernel selection layer, KV/prefix cache, model loader (cold/warm paths), telemetry & tracing, and runtime control plane. Each component is described below with ownership and SLO impact.

Components and responsibilities:
- Request Router (service: routerd) — routes by policy (latency, cost, region, model-variant). Owner: runtime-routing team. Impacts per-request P99.
- Batching Manager (service: batchd) — groups compatible requests, enforces SLOs and max-latency budgets, maintains dynamic batch-size histograms. Owner: batching team.
- Kernel Selection Layer — chooses CUDA/ROCm kernels and quantization execution paths per op and sequence length. Owner: kernels team.
- Executor & Scheduler — maps batches to GPU worker processes, enforces preemption and priority lanes. See kernel scheduling section.
- KV Cache & Prefix Cache — shared cache layer for repeated prompt prefixes and partial KV snapshots. Owner: cache team.
- Model Loader — multi-tier loader (cold, warm, pinned), handles weight quantization variants and memory reclamation.
- Telemetry & Tracing (service: runtime-telemetry) — emits per-token latency breakdown, memory stats, and kernel metrics. Integrates with Console dashboards and traces.

SLOs and impact matrix:
- API P99 latency SLO: 250ms (hosted small models), 600ms (large models where applicable)
- Throughput SLO: model-specific — documented per model in model-catalog
- Memory reclamation threshold: 80% of GPU memory triggers eviction/cold-unload procedures

2) Kernel scheduling design and policies
Design principles:
- Prioritize latency-critical small-batch requests while maintaining reasonable throughput for large-batch workloads.
- Avoid starvation: background batch jobs run on lower priority lanes and are preemptible.
- Predictability: scheduling decisions must be deterministic to aid debugging and regression detection.

Priority lanes and preemption rules (example):
- Lane: realtime-low => target_max_latency_ms=150, weight=100, preemptible=false
- Lane: realtime-high => target_max_latency_ms=350, weight=70, preemptible=false
- Lane: standard => target_max_latency_ms=800, weight=40, preemptible=true
- Lane: batch-background => target_max_latency_ms=5000, weight=10, preemptible=true

Example scheduling config table:
| Setting | Description | Default / Recommended |
|---------|-------------|-----------------------|
| max_inflight_per_gpu | Max concurrent batches on a single GPU | 8 |
| preemption_grace_ms | Minimum time before preemption allowed | 50 ms |
| time_slice_ms | Kernel execution time slice for fairness enforcement | 200 ms |
| kernel_selection_mode | static | dynamic | dynamic (use perf profiles) |

Preemption and fairness:
- Preemption is cooperative where possible: long-running kernels advertise preemption points (KV flush, attention chunk boundaries).
- Hard preemption is used only for batch-background lanes; it triggers checkpointing of partial KV state.

3) Profiling playbook (how-to for a perf investigation)
When you receive a latency/throughput regression or need baseline profiling, follow this playbook.

Quick steps (triage):
1. Reproduce with the canonical benchmarking harness (see section 4). Use the same model + quantization + seq_len used in production.
2. Collect traces and histograms for the offending timeframe: runtime token traces, worker-level metrics, GPU kernel timelines.
3. Compare with known-good baseline (tagged by commit and run id).

Command snippets and tools:
- Start system traces: agentctl trace --target=worker-12 --duration=60s --out=/tmp/trace-$(date +%s).nsys
- GPU timelines: nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --output=nsys-${RUN_ID} ./run_benchmark.sh
- Kernel flame graph (CPU side): perf record -g -p <pid> && perf script | flamegraph.pl > flame.svg
- Torch/TensorRT internal profiler: torch.profiler.profile(..., activities=[ProfilerActivity.CUDA, ProfilerActivity.CPU])

Metrics to collect (minimum):
- Per-token latency breakdown: queue_time, batch_wait_time, kernel_time, postprocess_time
- GPU memory high-water mark and fragmentation stats
- Kernel launch counts and average duration per op type (matmul, attention, softmax, layernorm)
- Scheduler decisions: batch_size, lane, preemption events

Profiling checklist (must include in ticket):
- Repro steps + exact benchmark command
- Run id(s) and git commit hash for runtime and kernels
- Collected artifacts: nsys trace, kernel logs, telemetry export (JSON), flame graphs
- Short summary with suspected root cause and recommended mitigation

4) Benchmarking suite and standards
Purpose:
Maintain stable, reproducible performance baselines across commits and releases. Benchmarks are used to: validate new kernel implementations, quantify quantization trade-offs, and measure scheduling policy changes.

Bench scenarios (representative):
- Latency-sensitive: 1–4 token prompts, batch sizes 1–8, seq_len 256
- Throughput-sensitive: steady stream, large batches up to 64, seq_len 1024
- Mixed/multi-tenant: heterogeneous mix matching production distribution (use traffic replay harness)

Result format and tagging:
All benchmark runs produce JSON results with flat fields: run_id, commit_hash, model, quantization, workload_profile, p50_ms, p95_ms, p99_ms, throughput_tok_s, gpu_util_pct. Results are uploaded to benchmarkdb and visible in Console.

CI integration:
- PRs touching kernels or scheduler must run the "bench-quick" job (subset of scenarios) and attach benchmark results to PR. The gating threshold is: no P99 regressions >5% on latency-sensitive profile.

5) Release notes & change log conventions (runtime & kernels)
Format (required for all runtime/kernels releases):
- Release: runtime-x.y.z (semantic version)
- Date: YYYY-MM-DD
- Notable changes: bullet list with short descriptions, risk categorization (low/medium/high), owners for rollback
- Bench summary: top-level P99/P95 deltas vs baseline commit

Example entry:
Release: runtime-2.14.0
Date: 2029-10-28
Notable changes:
- Dynamic kernel selection enabled by default for attention (owner: Kernels team) — risk: medium
- Fixed memory fragmentation in model loader that could cause cold-load OOMs — risk: low
Bench summary: p99(latency-sensitive) +1.2% (within tolerance)

Rollback plan must include explicit git tag and docker image tag and the following steps:
1. Pause rollout in Console for the affected cluster(s)
2. Trigger controlled rollback: platform-deploy rollback runtime runtime-2.13.9 --clusters cluster-a,cluster-b
3. Monitor telemetry for 30 minutes following rollback

6) Known issues (current high priority items)
- Issue: Large seq_len (>= 2048) + quantized int4 models can see elevated matmul kernel stalls under high multi-tenant load.
  - Impact: increased p99 latency by up to 300ms on affected clusters
  - Workaround: pin heavy customers to dedicated capacity or reduce max batch size to 16 for affected model variants
  - Owner: kernels-team
- Issue: KV cache eviction race condition during preemption events (found in 2.13.x)
  - Impact: rare correctness/regression in continuation tokens after preemption and immediate replay
  - Workaround: enable preemption-safe-kv in runtime config until 2.14.1
  - Owner: cache-team
- Issue: Occasional CUDA driver interactions causing worker process restart on Nvidia driver 532.x
  - Impact: transient errors, automatic restart recovers but increases tail latency
  - Workaround: upgrade driver to 535+ or use pinned nodes

7) Runtime runbooks (operational procedures)
Runbook: High P99 latency (alerts: runtime.p99_latency > SLO threshold for 15m)
1. Triage: confirm scope using Console: is it single-cluster, multi-cluster, or single model?
2. Check recent deploys: platform-deploy list --since 1h
3. Collect traces: agentctl snapshot --service=worker --since=10m --out=/tmp/snap-${INC_ID}.tar.gz
4. If lane saturation detected (batch-background hogging GPU), reduce background weight: runtime-config set scheduling.batch-background.weight 5
5. If kernel hotspots are present (attention matmul), open a perf ticket and attach nsys trace.
6. If no quick fix, enact escalation: paging kernels-team and SRE lead.

Runbook: OOM on model load
1. Identify node and process: monitor shows OOM events in node-exporter logs.
2. Attempt graceful unload: runtime-admin unload-model --model-id X --node Y
3. If unload fails, cordon node and trigger controlled restart: k8s cordon && restart worker pod.
4. Postmortem: include memory HWM and fragmentation graphs, model size and quantization variant used.

8) Team wiki & ownership
- Primary owners: serving-runtime (primary), kernels (kernel optimisations), batching (scheduling), cache (KV/prefix cache).
- Oncall: serving-runtime oncall rotation is listed in the team wiki (link: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/serving-runtime-oncall).
- Contacts for emergency escalation: runtime-sre-pager (Slack channel: #runtime-sre-pager).

Maintenance cadence and housekeeping:
- Monthly: bench full-suite against stable prod baseline, publish report to Console and the "perf-reports" channel.
- Quarterly: review scheduling policy defaults and lane weights.
- Before major kernel releases: run multi-tenant replay for 48h on staging and compare p99 distributions.

Appendix: Templates and config snippets
Scheduling config example (YAML):
---
scheduler:
  lanes:
    - name: realtime-low
      target_max_latency_ms: 150
      weight: 100
      preemptible: false
    - name: standard
      target_max_latency_ms: 800
      weight: 40
      preemptible: true
  max_inflight_per_gpu: 8
  preemption_grace_ms: 50
  time_slice_ms: 200
---

Benchmark run command (canonical):
./bench/harness/run_benchmark.sh --model gpt-redwood-7B --quant int8 --profile latency-sensitive --run-id ${RUN_ID} --out results/${RUN_ID}.json

Artifacts to attach when filing a perf/regression ticket:
- results/${RUN_ID}.json
- nsys-${RUN_ID}.qdrep and exported traces
- runtime-telemetry-${RUN_ID}.json
- short reproduction script and config

References and related pages:
